title: Sea depth between island and mainland predicts their mammalian affinity

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Sea depth between island and mainland predicts their mammalian affinity

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Somewhat independently of distance, the depth of sea separating an island from the neighbouring mainland is related to whether they share the same or allied mammal species: islands separated by shallow channels have the same or very similar mammals, those across deep water have distinct species and genera.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: there is also a relation, to a certain extent independent of distance, between the depth of the sea separating an island from the neighbouring mainland, and the presence in both of the same mammiferous species or of allied species in a more or less modified condition.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XII, “Geographical Distribution, continued”; section “Absence of Batrachians and of terrestrial Mammals”. Scope: terrestrial mammals of continental and near-continental islands

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch12-11: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.82

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The variables have direct modern measures and suitable global databases. Historical connectivity and correlated geography limit causal discrimination, but stratified sensitivity analyses are feasible.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For continental islands, model mammal taxonomic or phylogenetic similarity to the nearest mainland against channel depth while controlling for distance, island area and climate. A persistent negative depth effect confirms the claim; no effect or the opposite refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Introductions and incomplete island inventories can distort affinity.

Present bathymetry may differ from channels exposed at past low sea levels.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Depth, distance, species lists and phylogenetic relatedness are standard variables, and the partial-regression criterion follows the claim's 'independent of distance' wording directly. Open bathymetry, mammal range maps and a dated mammal tree cover most continental islands, with weaker native-status data for small islands. The comparison is a routine spatial analysis, though land-bridge history and introductions keep it from being fully clean.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For continental and near-continental islands, regress terrestrial-mammal species sharing and mean phylogenetic distance to the nearest mainland on minimum intervening sea depth, with geographic distance and island area held constant. The claim is confirmed if greater depth still predicts fewer shared species and more distant allies, and refuted if depth adds no partial association or the slope reverses.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Introduced mammals and incomplete native inventories can inflate or deflate apparent sharing.

Modern depth is an imperfect stand-in for Pleistocene land connections, because channels shallower than past lowstands were periodically dry.

Island area, climate and human history remain confounded with depth even after distance is controlled.

fields.value:

data existence: 0.8

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Across continental and near-continental islands, the fraction of an island's terrestrial mammal species that also occur on the neighbouring mainland decreases with the maximum depth of the sea channel separating them, and this relationship holds after controlling for the width of the channel; islands whose channel is shallower than the Pleistocene low stand (about 120 m) share more species than islands whose channel is deeper.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: For each of 28 islands the GBIF occurrence API returned speciesKey and genusKey facet counts for Mammalia in the island box and in the mainland box, and the same for Chiroptera, Cetacea, Sirenia, Phocidae, Otariidae, Odobenidae and 12 domestic or commensal genera, which were subtracted; species with >= 3 records formed the sets. f = fraction of island species also present in the mainland set. Channel depth = greatest depth among 100 GEBCO 2020 points along the pre-registered straight transect (OpenTopoData API); width = transect length. Three islands with < 5 qualifying species (Pemba, Lombok, Cyprus) were dropped (n = 25). Spearman's rho between f and log depth, the partial Spearman correlation controlling log width, and the shallow (<= 120 m) vs deep (> 120 m) means were compared with the pre-registered thresholds.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: for each of 28 fixed islands, (i) the terrestrial mammal species set (GBIF Mammalia occurrences with >= 3 records inside the island box, minus bats, cetaceans, sirenians, pinnipeds and 12 domestic or commensal genera), (ii) the same for a fixed neighbouring-mainland box, (iii) channel depth = greatest water depth (GEBCO 2020 via the OpenTopoData API, 100 points) along a fixed straight transect between the nearest island and mainland shores, and (iv) channel width = transect length. f = |island ∩ mainland| / |island|. SUPPORTS if all of: Spearman rho(f, log depth) < 0 with one-sided p < 0.05; partial Spearman of f on log depth controlling log width < 0 with one-sided p < 0.05; mean f of islands with depth <= 120 m exceeds mean f of islands with depth > 120 m.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: REFUTES if Spearman rho(f, log depth) >= 0 or if mean f of shallow (<= 120 m) islands is <= mean f of deep (> 120 m) islands. Any other outcome is MIXED. Islands with fewer than 5 qualifying species are dropped; with fewer than 12 islands remaining the result is inconclusive (underpowered). If the bathymetry API is unreachable the result is inconclusive (data-unavailable).

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: Spearman rho between log channel depth and the fraction of island terrestrial mammal species shared with the neighbouring mainland

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: one-sided p=0.139; partial rho controlling log channel width=-0.116, one-sided p=0.295

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: 'Terrestrial mammals' excludes bats (Darwin treats them separately), marine mammals and species carried by humans (domestic stock, commensal rodents, Homo); other introductions remain in GBIF and bias against the claim by making deep-water islands look similar to the mainland. 'Depth of sea' is the present maximum depth along a straight line between the nearest shores; Darwin's reasoning is about former land connections, so the 120 m Pleistocene low-stand depth is the pre-registered dividing line, and present depth is an imperfect stand-in for past connection (caveat). 'Same or allied species' is measured at the species level only (shared species fraction); genus-level affinity is recorded as a secondary descriptive measure. For Wallacean islands (Sulawesi, Lombok) the Sunda-shelf islands Borneo and Bali serve as the 'mainland', and for Hokkaido and Ireland the larger neighbouring islands (Honshu, Great Britain) do, as Darwin himself discusses Britain and its islands; this is noted.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
GBIF occurrence search API (facet counts of speciesKey/genusKey for Mammalia and excluded groups within island and mainland boxes; GBIF Backbone Taxonomy for keys)

GEBCO 2020 global bathymetry grid, sampled through the OpenTopoData public API (dataset gebco2020)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The direction is as Darwin stated (rho = -0.23; shallow islands share 59% of species with the mainland, deep islands 50%; the three deepest continental fragments, Cuba, Sulawesi and Madagascar, share 9%, 5% and 1%), but neither the correlation nor the shallow-deep difference reaches the pre-registered significance levels, so the verdict is MIXED.

The deep-water islands with high sharing are the Mediterranean islands (Corsica-Sardinia 0.72, Crete 0.73, Balearics 0.81, Sicily 0.39) plus Ireland (0.94) and Vancouver Island (0.86). The Mediterranean islands' present mammal faunas consist overwhelmingly of species introduced by humans since the Neolithic after their endemic faunas went extinct, and Ireland's fauna includes many Holocene introductions; GBIF has no reliable native-status flag, so these introductions could not be removed and they work directly against the claim. Vancouver Island was glaciated and its present channel depth overstates its Pleistocene isolation.

Several shallow-channel islands show low sharing for reasons unrelated to depth: New Guinea (0.20) and Sulawesi-adjacent Borneo (0.52) have large endemic radiations and small mainland reference boxes; Taiwan (0.36), Hainan (0.33) and Bioko (0.39) carry many island forms raised to species rank in recent taxonomy, which lowers species-level sharing while genus-level sharing stays higher (Hokkaido 0.47 vs 0.90 at genus level).

Channel depth is the maximum depth along one straight line between two pre-registered points, not the true sill depth; several transects cross land (e.g. 70 of 100 points for Sakhalin, 59 for Trinidad), and present depth is only a proxy for Pleistocene connection, which is what Darwin's argument actually concerns.

For Sulawesi and Lombok the Sunda-shelf islands Borneo and Bali stand in for the mainland, and for Hokkaido and Ireland the larger neighbouring islands do.

Bounding boxes of very different size and sampling intensity were used for islands and mainland regions; a mainland box that is too small or too thinly recorded lowers f regardless of depth.

GBIF is a live resource; re-running reproduces the method but counts drift as records are added.
